--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.add_gn_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Add a growing network (GN): a random tree grown by degree-biased attachment. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.add_gn_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Add a growing network (GN): a random tree grown by degree-biased attachment. title: >- [Graph.add_gn_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Add a growing network (GN): a random tree grown by degree-biased attachment. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Add a growing network (GN): a random tree grown by degree-biased attachment. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L14357-L14505){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.add_gn_graph( n, kernel=None, seed=None, type=None, label=True, rel=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Growing network](../assets/graphs/add-gn-graph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three growing networks on eight nodes, drawn as trees with the first node at the top and every arc pointing from a newer node to the older node it attached to. With a constant kernel the target is uniform and the first node gets 3 arcs; with the default linear kernel it gets 5; with the kernel k**2 the rich get richer so fast that all 7 later nodes point at it." width="100%"} Starts with two linked nodes and adds the rest one at a time. Each new node makes one edge, to an existing node chosen with probability proportional to `kernel(degree)`. The default kernel is the degree itself, which is linear preferential attachment (the Barabási-Albert model with one edge per node) and gives a power-law degree distribution. A superlinear kernel such as `lambda d: d ** 1.5` lets one hub win nearly every new link, while a sublinear one such as `lambda d: d ** 0.5` gives a distribution with a lighter, stretched-exponential tail. The model is due to Krapivsky and Redner; the process follows NetworkX's `gn_graph()`. Each edge points from the new node to the older node it attached to, so in a directed graph every node but the first has one out-edge and all paths lead to the first node. In an undirected graph the same edges are added without their direction. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. GN graphs are useful for: - modeling citation-like growth, where each item points to one earlier item - studying how the attachment kernel shapes the degree distribution - random directed trees rooted at the oldest node ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes. [kernel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[Callable[[int], float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Function giving the attachment weight of a node from its degree (counting both directions). It is called once for each degree from `0` to `n - 1` before the growth starts and must return finite, non-negative numbers. If `None` (default), the weight is the degree. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same other arguments always gives the same graph. If `None` (default), the graph differs on every call. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n=` is negative, `kernel=` returns a negative or non-finite weight, or every existing node has zero weight when a target must be chosen. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~add_gnr_graph`) : Grow a tree by redirecting links instead of using a kernel. [](`~add_gnc_graph`) : Grow a denser graph in which new nodes copy links. [](`~add_pa_graph`) : Grow an undirected graph by preferential attachment. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Each new node links to one existing node, so every node but the first has exactly one out-edge, and `100` nodes have `99` edges: ::: {#6ca84975 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_gn_graph(n=100, seed=7) out_degrees = {graph.get_out_degree(v) for v in graph.get_node_ids()} graph.count_edges(), out_degrees ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (99, {0, 1}) ``` ::: ::: The kernel maps an existing node's degree to its weight as a target. The default is linear; a sublinear kernel spreads the links out, and a superlinear one concentrates them on one hub. The largest degree for each: ::: {#93944abc .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def largest_degree(kernel): g = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_gn_graph(n=100, kernel=kernel, seed=7) return max(g.degrees(return_dict=True).values()) [largest_degree(k) for k in (lambda d: d**0.5, None, lambda d: d**2)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [9, 23, 97] ``` ::: ::: ### A linear kernel or a superlinear one Thirty nodes with the default linear kernel on the left and the kernel `d**2` on the right. Both are trees with every edge pointing toward older nodes, but with the squared kernel almost every node links straight to one hub: ::: {#e8eaf46b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} linear = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_gn_graph(n=30, seed=7) squared = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_gn_graph( n=30, kernel=lambda d: d**2, seed=7 ) def largest_in_degree(g): return max(g.get_in_degree(v) for v in g.get_node_ids()) largest_in_degree(linear), largest_in_degree(squared) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (13, 28) ``` ::: ::: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#6ba4754d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} linear.plot( show_labels=False, node_size=6, width=320, height=320, legend=False, seed=1, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
